Mr. Speaker, today many hundreds of Indian people, most of them young, rallied on Parliament Hill to protest vigorously the Government's decision to limit and restrict its spending on education for Indian and Inuit students.
Thousands of young Indian and Inuit students will be unable to pursue post-secondary education this year because of the Government's complex system of capping expenditures and creating categories of eligibility. Funds for primary and secondary education are being shifted here and there across the country, and Quebec is about to lose nearly $3 million in the process.
Indian control of Indian education is proceeding at a snail's pace. When there is a transfer of responsibility, it is with fewer resources than when it was retained under government control.
1 say, Sir, to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. McKnight), and to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), re-examine your spending priorities. I ask, do not cast aside yet another generation of aboriginal young people.
Six thousand one hundred and thirty-nine Indian people have signed documents urging the Government of Canada to fulfil its treaty and trust obligations, and provide the necessary educational funding. Those signatures will be delivered this afternoon to the Prime Minister's Office. The Indian people of Canada do expect a positive response.

Mr. Speaker, 10 years ago the House of Commons was introduced to the heat of television lights and the ever watchful eye of automated cameras. During the past decade the House of Commons has been trivialized by being televised. The new medium has brought a new message.
The televising of House of Commons Question Period has reinterpreted the rule book without rewriting the rules. The rule of relevance is vanishing. The notion that questions ought not to be argumentative has given way to the new medium that demands heat and attack.
No longer is substance the essence of politics. Very few people measure the warrant, the premise, the presumptions, or the evidence upon which conclusions are drawn. The new medium encourages unsubstantiated accusations. Cute expressions have become a substitute for research. Shrillness and high drama are characteristics that are observably more present than a decade ago.
Parliament, citizens, and the process of thoughtful democracy have been the losers. Our nation and her citizens have turned more negative. Accomplishments are seldom applauded, because in every great achievement there is, no matter how small, a dark phase to be exploited, and television drama and exploitation are synonymous. Television has reduced our character and diminished our procedures.
Ah, TV or not TV, that is the question.
Whether 'tis is nobler in the mind to suffer the slings and arrows of outrageous comment, or by opposing end them . . . Et tu, Brute\

Mr. Speaker, this afternoon the 1987 Persons Awards will be presented to five outstanding Canadian women to honour their contributions toward improving the status of women in Canada.

October 21, 1987
The "Persons Case" was won on October 18, 1929, by a group of suffragists known as "The Famous Five". Led by Judge Emily Murphy, the first woman magistrate in the British Empire, this group of Alberta women included Louise McKinney, Nellie McClung, Irene Parlby, and Elenrietta Muir Edwards. Together they fought to have women defined as persons under the law and succeeded in their struggle.

I want to ask you to join me in celebrating the anniversary of this remarkable achievement by paying tribute to the women who have followed in the footsteps of the Famous Five: Jacqueline Laprise-Demers, Margaret Catherine Harris, Frances Laracy, Kay Macpherson and Norma Walmsley. It is very encouraging to see that their efforts to improve women's social economic status have been acknowledged by the Canadian Government. I hope this recognition will inspire other women to take part in the struggle to improve the status of Canadian women.

As Rosemary Brown once said, "Until all of us have made it, none of us have made it".

Mrs. Becker was 54 when the Supreme Court awarded her half the assets she had earned while sharing the life of her spouse for twenty years on a farm in Valleyfield. When the court handed out its judgment in December, 1980, Mrs. Becker was happy that she had helped advance the cause of women through this particular case. When she died six years later, she was working as a maid on a farm in Valleyfield and had yet to obtain a single penny of the money she had been awarded, and all because her lawyer had taken his own fee before handing over the money she had been awarded. She left a message, asking the women of Canada and the Government to change the legislation so that when a similar judgment is handed down, the money and assets are give to the client before the lawyers can take out their own fees.
We wish to pay tribute to Mrs. Rosa Becker and to all women in similar situations.

CANADA-UNITED STATES TRADE AGREEMENT-EFFECT ON CAPE BRETON
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the people of Cape Breton whose economy is so dependent upon the operations of two Crown corporations are very concerned about the potentially devastating effects of the Government's trade deal with the United States.
The Cape Breton Development Corporation sells coal to the Nova Scotia Power Corporation under a special arrangement to protect the jobs of Cape Breton workers. This underground coal is more expensive to produce than American coal and would not be competitive.
Sydney Steel, a provincial Crown corporation, receives preferential treatment from Canadian National and from the Canadian International Development Agency in the purchase of steel rails for use in Canada as well as internationally.
Because the Government has agreed with the United States to open government procurement to competition from the United States and because the Government has also agreed to take measures to ensure compliance by provincial and local authorities, there is an urgent need for the Government to clarify this issue. It should tell the people of Cape Breton and of Canada whether provincial and federal Crown corporations and federal government agencies, such as CIDA, will be required to purchase from the lowest bidder, whether American or Canadian, or whether they will be prevented from operating such programs which support jobs and industry in the regions of Canada desperately needing government action to assist in economic development.

subsubtopic: PROPOSED CONSTRUCTION OF ETHANOL PLANT IN DAWSON CREEK, B.C.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Agri-Fuels Canada Limited is planning to construct a $90 million ethanol plant in Dawson Creek, B.C. A large portion of the required grain will come from farms located in the Alberta Peace country. The use of ethanol in gasoline has many advantages. The opportunity for farmers to market their grain would create jobs, keep people on the farms and stimulate economic activity to help farmers through these difficult times. The use of ethanol would also result in a cleaner, safer environment.
The market currently exists for ethanol in Alaska. However, in order to ensure the success of the plant, action must be taken to secure a Canadian market. The Minister of State for Science and Technology (Mr. Oberle), who has worked hard to ensure this project's success, advised me that Petro-Canada should be making a decision this week on the use of ethanol in its product.
I strongly urge Petro-Canada officials to come to a positive decision to use ethanol from the Dawson Creek plant as a fuel additive.

October 21, 1987

apply against Canada. He then said that the so-called dispute mechanism: "guarantees fair and impartial application of respective laws", but went on to say that the mechanism would not deal with "fine points of law".

1.	The Constitution Act, 1867 is amended by adding thereto, immediately after section 1 thereof, the following section:

Mr. Speaker, when I spoke on Monday, I was comparing the position taken by the New Democratic Party at our convention in Montreal in March when we had arrived at the end of a lengthy period of reflection on the question of Quebec and Canada with the actual terms of the Meech Lake Accord.
We called for the Constitution to recognize the uniqueness of Quebec, and the Accord recognizes that Quebec constitutes a distinct society. We said in our resolution, in our Party policy, that Quebec should be able to opt out with compensation if there was any transfer of provincial powers to the federal level with which it disagreed. That is contained in one of the provisions of the Accord. We said that Quebec should have a veto on any amendment that would alter federal institutions when these were considered vital to the security and preservation of the French language and culture in Quebec. As you know, the Accord provides that there is in fact a veto to every province because of the rule of unanimity for changes in federal institutions.
The fourth part of our resolution, which as I say was arrived at after a great deal of sober and serious reflection, wanted the Party to explore new constitutional provisions. The purpose would be to protect the linguistic rights of Quebec's majority

October 21, 1987
Constitution Amendment, 1987
while at the same time ensuring the preservation of minority language rights as they now exist in the Constitution. We were not exactly sure how to do that, and put it aside for further study.
1 regret that the Premiers were unable to resolve this particular issue in their discussions at Meech Lake and in the Langevin Block. I believe this is a matter which should be dealt with in the future because, as Quebec has indicated through Bill 101 and by other means, there are particular requirements in that province as a French speaking island in a North American continent which speaks English, where the protection of the language of the majority as well as the protection of minority language rights should be sought.
There can be no question about the fact that New Democrats have concerns over the Accord. I share those concerns. But we have to put these in context with the fact that Quebec is saying yes to Confederation. It is in that spirit that 1 support the Accord and intend to vote for it when it comes to the vote next Monday.
Nonetheless, I and my colleagues share the concern that the Accord passes over the question of whether or not the rights that were won after such a battle by women at the time of the constitutional agreements of six or seven years ago might be downgraded by the Accord. Our experts, our members, who sat on the joint committee, did not believe that. It is not our position or belief that that is the case, but in order to ensure that that does not take place, and in response to the concerns of women's groups across Canada, we believe that the Accord should specifically ensure that women's rights are not overridden by these provisions.
We are concerned that the Accord completely ignores the essential requirement that the Constitution of Canada be amended in order to deal with legitimate concerns of Canada's aboriginal peoples. I believe the commitment at the last round, that there be a constitutional conference on aboriginal peoples and rights, should have been reiterated in the Accord.
We are concerned that one province could veto the Yukon and Northwest Territories from becoming a province sometime in the future.
We are concerned that a northerner cannot be named to the Supreme Court of Canada. We believe that that should be fixed now rather than being left.
I have to say that, given the recent difficulties, perhaps as well the Accord should be amended now in order to curtail for a limited period of time the powers of the Senate of Canada to block legislation that has been adopted by the Parliament of Canada.
When I hear other complaints about the Accord I have to say that I fail to find them convincing. It has been suggested that Canada is becoming balkanized and yet powers are not redistributed in the Accord. It has been suggested that the spending power will no longer be a useful tool for the federal Government, despite the fact that the spending power is being
recognized for the first time in the Constitution, according to the terms of the Accord. It is only where we are talking about a shared program in an area of provincial jurisdiction and where a province puts in place a program that meets the national objectives that a province will be able to enjoy the financial compensation which is called for in the Accord. That is a very narrow set of requirements, Mr. Speaker. It is still open for the federal Government to use its spending power exclusively, rather than on a shared basis, in order to act in an area which is largely of provincial jurisdiction.
The question here is the nature of the country. I believe that Canada has to operate co-operatively. I was here in this Parliament as an observer, as a journalist in the 1960s. I have seen the development of the provincial levels of Government in the past 20 years during my active career as a journalist and as a politician. The provinces have much more competence than they had back in those days. They have a much greater share in spending and in the provision of social services. They are closer to being equal partners with the federal Government than they were at the beginning of the 1960s. I do not think there is anything wrong in recognizing that in a constitutional Accord, which at the same time reserves the essential powers already there for a federal Government.
My Party, however, recognizes that we cannot run Canada, a country which is 4,000 miles in breadth, as though it were a centralized small state like the United Kingdom of England, Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland. We must have decentralization. Everybody acknowledges that whether we are talking about regional development policy, economic development policy or the Constitution. I believe we have the right balance in the Accord.
Some people have expressed concern over the provisions recognizing Quebec as a distinct society. I simply say to them that the New Democratic Party since its foundation in 1961 has sought to recognize the uniqueness of Quebec. We have used a number of different formulae but we have not wavered in our recognition that Quebec is a unique society. Yes, of course, that can create some difficulties.
If the alternative is not to have a country that is whole, then surely we must recognize what observers have said from the beginning of the foundation of our country, that having a part of Canada where French is the language and culture of the majority is something unique and distinct and it should be recognized in the Constitution.
It has been suggested that because of the rule of unanimity we are freezing constitutional reform. I disagree. The fact is that most amendments to the Constitution can continue to be made on the basis of the majority plus seven provinces. The rule of unanimity only applies to certain areas where it did not apply before, namely, to the area of federal institutions. I regret that perhaps this makes the process of Senate reform more difficult. The process of the abolition of the Senate will
October 21, 1987

be more difficult. Nonetheless, we can get to that later. We are bringing Quebec in right now and we are not stopping the power of the majority of the provinces, for example, to change the allocation of powers between the federal and provincial levels if that is what they want to do.
I have already dealt with the question of women's rights. I want to note, however, that both the National Action Committee on the Status of Women and the Federation des femmes du Quebec agree with the position that with an abundance of caution, there should be a saving clause. I would hope that Members of all Parties would accept that particular amendment by the New Democratic Party.
I want to conclude by speaking about two important decisions which are now before this Parliament and this country. First is the issue of the Meech Lake Accord, the constitutional amendments, and the second is the issue of free trade. I want to talk about the process that is taking place in those two particular questions.
It is now some 25 years since the beginning of the quiet revolution, 30 years since the beginning of the quiet revolution in Quebec. It is 25 years since Canadians have begun to actively ask, "What does Quebec want?" as it was phrased in Ontario, and to work in different ways to find a new basis for partnership between the rest of Canada and French-speaking Canadians in the Province of Quebec.
When we embarked on constitutional change in 1981, it was after a referendum in Quebec in which Quebecers spoke in favour of Canada, but that was on the basis of a pledge by Canadians from the rest of the country that real action would be taken. Now we have a second run and real action is being taken. The Meech Lake Accord follows proposals made first by Premier Levesque and then by Premier Bourassa. It follows lengthy negotiations. It follows a process of discussion by the premiers as well as by their representatives. It will not be ratified until it has been endorsed by this Parliament and by the legislature of every province. The process has been criticized by the select committee, by the joint committee. Nonetheless, there has been a lengthy process in which every Canadian could become involved, and this for a document of only 12 pages.
When the President of the United States said two and a half weeks ago that Canada and the United States have signed the basis of a new economic constitution for North America, have signed what amounts to an economic union between Canada and the United States, and I look at the process which is being followed, I am ashamed of the Government. I am ashamed of my country that we should enter into this agreement with such a faulty process.
If we sign an extradition treaty with the Republic of India, for example, it is done by the normal executive powers which the Government of the day sustains through having the confidence of the House of Commons. However, there was no mandate for the free trade agreement in the 1984 election. In fact, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) spoke against it in
Constitution Amendment, 1987
running for the leadership of his Party back in the early 1980s. There has been no mandate from the people of Canada to have an economic union with the United States.
In previous years, in the 1870s, in 1911, and again after the Second World War, the prospects of economic union was discussed, considered and in one case went to an election, and Canadians indicated that they did not want to lose sovereignty. Of course, there has been a cost. We have lost, perhaps, in terms of our standards of living. Perhaps a few products from United States have not been available in Canadian stores. But we have gained in terms of our nationhood, in terms of the fact that we have done things differently, and that Quebec can now find a place within Canada which it could never find within a unified new nation comprising Canada and the United States. What we have gained is without comparison.
I believe we had better put it on the line and say that it is wrong to let the sovereignty of this country go down the drain without at least giving the people of Canada a chance to speak.
I am not afraid, as some members of the Government have suggested, for Canada to go it alone if this is a bad deal. I am not afraid to take the risk of Canada standing on its own, because we have stood alone for 120 years since Confederation. We have often been threatened with absorption by our neighbour to the south and we have withstood that successfully. 1 am proud of what we have achieved as Canadians and I believe that Canadians are confident enough to continue in that way if we cannot get a decent kind of arrangement with the United States.
I believe this country must have the chance to speak on the Meech Lake Accord, and we are speaking, through our parliaments and through our legislatures. The people of Canada have had a chance to say, yes, they want Quebec in. The people of Canada have not had that chance with respect to the free trade agreement. I believe that before the free trade agreement is entered into there must be an election in which all Canadians can speak. and later up to 1979, fully expected that there would be changes in the distribution of power.
Perhaps the most controversial aspect of the Accord is the inclusion of two interpretative clauses, namely, that the Constitution is to be interpreted in a manner consistent with linguistic duality across the country, which has been described as a fundamental characteristic of Canada, and with the recognition of Quebec as a distinct society. These principles must be taken into account by the courts along with other rules of interpretation in arriving at a decision on a given set of facts.
As a matter of law, the linguistic duality and distinct society clauses neither grant new powers nor derogate from existing powers. An interpretative clause by definition cannot breathe life into a jurisdiction that does not exist.
The Accord recognizes that within Canada, Quebec is a distinct society. This recognition is appropriate, not only because it is historically and sociologically true but because Quebec's distinct society has already been acknowledged by the courts. The Accord does make explicit what has been implicit in our laws and constitutional arrangements for over 250 years.
It must be remembered that Quebec's distinct society includes not only the French-speaking majority but also the English-speaking minority, the aboriginal people in northern Quebec and the rich and diverse communities of other cultures and traditions.
How, then, will the distinct society clause work? How does it come to have any meaning? In the view of the distinguished constitutional experts who appeared before the committee, the distinct society clause will have an influence on Section 1 of the Charter.
For example, when a Quebec statute is challenged as being inconsistent with some Charter principle, if the court decides that there is an inconsistency or a violation of that Charter value the court will then be compelled to decide whether the provision of the statute can be saved as a reasonable limitation in a free and democratic society. This is a process that constitutional lawyers go through every day before the courts. The court would make that decision using as one factor the linguistic duality, distinct society interpretative clauses in the Accord.
The distinct society provision has not been specifically defined. But then, such phrases as "reasonable limits prescribed by law as can be demonstrably justified in a free and democratic society", which is in the 1982 Constitution has not been defined. The phrase "peace, order and good government" and "property and civil rights" have not been defined with any sense of precision in the past. It has been left to the courts to interpret those phrases in a socially relevant fashion. In due course, a body of jurisprudence will develop which will put contours around the meaning of such phrases.
