I wish to now turn to another provision on the same point of the need for expanding co-operation between the federal Government and the provinces, and the provinces with each other, which is the suggestion that we will be having regular conferences to discuss constitutional reform. In the future, hopefully we will not have to have them because they are dealing, quite literally, with the crisis of unity of the country. If we do institutionalize such conferences-and I will have some more to say about the need to have Canadians participate more directly-hopefully when a problem begins to emerge, at the regular annual conference that discusses constitutional change, the federal Government and the provinces will come together and be able to address the need for change before a problem becomes a crisis. Again, I think that that provision is a good one, and it will be conducive to the spirit and reality of co-operative federalism.
The next aspect of this Accord that I wish to say something about is the Charter of Rights. I wish to say at the outset that my Party would not support the Accord if we believed the rights of Canadians under the Charter were overridden in any way by this Accord. I say in this context that the Charter
remains, and it remains as strong after this Accord as it was before this Accord was introduced.
Hear, hear!

Notwithstanding our belief that the Accord will be good for Canada, we do have some serious concerns and objections. For that reason we have proposed some amendments. I wish to mention at the outset the reasoning that lay behind those amendments.
When any group of Canadians in any of Canada's political Parties receive a constitutional document, and one does not need to be lawyer to do this type of thing, they can find lots of things wrong with it after perusal of some 20 seconds. I am tempted to say if one is a New Democrat, it can normally be done after five seconds, but I will not say that.
The serious point I wish to make is that any constitutional document that one has will always be short of what a person in good faith can deem to be desirable in terms of additional conclusions. We all have an agenda and a favourable item that we wish to have included in a major proposal for constitutional change.
When my Party addressed this Accord it was aware of the plethora of proposals that could be made to add to it. We are also very conscious of the fact that the document was prepared with care, thought about with prudence, and that it is absolutely essential to gain acceptance in the early future by the Parliament of Canada and all provinces. Therefore, we did not want to propose a whole extended range of amendments. That was an important part of our thinking. The number of amendments we had in mind had to be few in number and had to be, of course, totally consistent with the Accord itself. Therefore, we proposed three of them, and I want to speak briefly on each.
The first one was on aboriginal rights. I do not think there ought to be a Member of Parliament who, at this point in our time as a nation, should be ignorant of the moral need to act and to act with speed in redressing the legitimate moral concerns of our aboriginal peoples.
Hear, hear!

The reality is that in the last Constitution go-around in 1982 we in Parliament entrenched aboriginal rights. It was a historic battle in the many stages of the process, but it was a historic accomplishment at the time. Many of us believed that by the time we got to this round certain specific rights of our aboriginal people needed to be addressed in a further more comprehensive way and, specifically, that the long overdue right of aboriginal Canadians to have some form of self-government ought to be put in place.
Therefore, it was with regret that we did not see a commitment in the Accord to have a further conference on this subject when we had commitments to have further conferences on
October 21, 1987

other subjects which, if I can put it this way, are certainly no more important than the claims of our aboriginal peoples. We have an amendment which deals with that, and it deals with the rights of aboriginal peoples themselves to participate in those conferences which will come up with a settlement of a number of claims, particularly the moral claim of establishing a form of aboriginal self-government in the country.
The second area of concern was the injustice which is now being foisted upon Canadians in the northern part of our land. It is a sad irony, in one sense, that we should be going from a form of isolation in our Constitution of the people of Quebec to imposing another kind of isolation upon Canadians in the North. This is completely unacceptable to my Party. Frankly we do not understand. 1 have written to the provincial Premiers and to the Prime Minister, and I cannot understand why we cannot get an amendment, even at this point, which would redress this grievance before we put it in place with this Accord. It is this injustice which is now being imposed upon the people of the Northwest Territories and the Yukon, both with regard to the process of becoming a province and to their right to participate equally with other Canadians in the selection of Supreme Court judges and Senators.
I repeat that the best way of dealing with one injustice for one part of Canada is not simultaneously to impose another injustice on another part of Canada.
Our third amendment deals with the equality rights of women. We in my Party do not believe that the linguistic duality-distinct society interpretation clause abrogates, supersedes, or overrides sexual equality rights or any other rights guaranteed by the Charter of Rights and Freedoms. However, I add immediately-and on Persons Day how symbolically appropriate it is to be making this point-that in earlier debates and discussions in the development of the Accord some of us said that no matter how remote or how unlikely an adverse effect of the distinct society clause would be in respect of aboriginal rights or our multicultural heritage, Sections 25 and 27 of the Charter should be included in Section 16 of the Accord, as we said, out of an abundance of caution.
As Hon. Members of the House will know, this change was made. We believe that the reasoning or concerns held by Canadians who were sensitive to the possible abrogation of aboriginal rights and multicultural rights were addressed. However, if it was legitimate to make a change to address those concerns, even though we did not believe those rights threatened, surely we ought to be making the same changes as this affects the rights of women. The same abundance of caution should be applied to sexual equality rights. This, in our judgment, could once again be done without in any sense jeopardizing the Accord.
I suppose in this context I would like to make a special appeal to the Premier of the Province of Quebec and to the other Premiers to give some serious second thought to accepting an amendment on this important point.
Constitution Amendment, 1987
The equality rights of women in the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms were won, incredibly as it may seem, a mere five years ago through a collective struggle. Again to be frank, it was really initiated and carried through by the women of Canada themselves who, by force of their argument and force of their concern, made the rest of us listen. The great struggle they had, which was carried on subsequently in the House of Commons, led to the establishment of Section 28 in our Constitution. It is a matter of which we as Canadians should be proud. Section 28 does for Canadian women what the United States has yet to do for women in the United States. We can be showing leadership in this regard, and in showing leadership, I say to the Prime Minister in this context, I hope he will give some consideration to accepting the kind of amendment we favour, which would reassure Canadian women on this important point and at the same time be totally consistent with the Accord before us.
I would now like to say a few words about some further proposals for future constitutional reform.

I would first like to say a few words about the Charter. Several groups that appeared before the committee expressed concerns that went beyond the scope of the 1987 Constitutional Accord.
The concerns of national womens' groups and their constitutional experts, of visible minority groups and others arose, for instance, from the legal interpretation of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms during the first five years of its existence. We must maintain the guarantees for the rights and freedoms of Canadians, including equality rights. A review of the Charter requires considerable participation on the part of the public and sufficient funding to enable all Canadians to make their views and concerns known.
Representatives of our visible minorities presented to the committee some convincing arguments about the need to examine, above all, Section 33 of the Charter, the "notwithstanding" section. We believe that Canada will not have an egalitarian society until the Charter's guarantees equality for minorities can no longer be compromised. We therefore suggest that a future first ministers' conference consider repealing Section 33.

We also agree whole-heartedly with representatives of ethnocultural associations who, in welcoming the Accord, stressed that constitutional recognition should also be given to Canada's ethnocultural reality as a fundamental characteristic of Canada. We too think that should be done.
The Canadians making these suggestions emphasized that one-third of Canadians are of neither English nor French origin. The Charter already recognizes Canada's multicultural heritage, and it is time that we moved one step further in the constitutional evolution of our country.

October 21, 1987
Constitution Amendment, 1987
I urge the First Ministers to move quickly to recognize in the Constitution Canada's ethnocultural reality as a fundamental characteristic of our nation.
New Democrats also agree with those who told the committee that Canadians must more directly be involved in future constitution making. The Constitution, after all, belongs to all Canadians, not just to the politicians here in the House of Commons or in the provinces. We must have a process that permits the people of Canada to participate in the discussion of constitutional reform before First Ministers deal with certain matters, and not just after. We want changes made in that direction.
I want to conclude with this observation. As I have indicated, the work done by the First Ministers, including the Prime Minister, and the committee that studied this question, has been a first rate job for the people of Canada. The Accord, as many Canadians have said both in this House and outside, is not a perfect document. But this constitutional Accord is a good document, good for Canada, good for Quebec, good for all the other provinces and good for individual citizens who want their rights preserved. We need to support it.
Hear, hear!

But I say this, that constitutions, no matter how good, do not cause progressive change in themselves. Constitutions lay the framework that permits active men and women to bring about changes that will make Canada a more just and compassionate nation. What is needed, in my view, is the political will now to act within a newly established constitution to achieve these goals.
With this reconciliation of monumental importance with the Province of Quebec and with the renewal of co-operative federalism, we must now strive together to make a better tomorrow for all Canadians.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Are there any questions or comments? Resuming debate. The Right Hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney).

Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak on the resolution on the Meech Lake Accord which brings Quebec back into the constitutional fold, which strengthens national unity and unblocks the process of future constitutional reform.
May I commend the Leader of the New Democratic Party today both for the excellence of his comments and the generous outlook he has taken on the problem of constitutional reform. While I was absent, my right hon. friend, the Leader
of the Opposition (Mr. Turner), spoke and I commend him as well for the leadership that he has adopted on a very sensitive national issue.
Hear, hear!

I have recommended this Accord to my colleagues in the Government. I recommend it today without reservation or qualification to all of my colleagues in the House of Commons. I commend it as well to future generations of Canadians, confident that the Accord will stand the test of time and the scrutiny of history.
Eleven First Ministers from four political Parties support this Accord.

The three national leaders of Canada's political parties in the House support it as well. Today, I sincerely invite all Hon. Members to join with us in this unique act of nation building, in saying "yes" to Quebec, "yes" to Canada, and "yes" to future constitutional reform.
Hear, hear!

1 want to speak today, briefly and from the heart, as a Quebecer and as a Canadian. Our constitution, the fundamental law of the land, is more than words on paper. It defines the terms of our living together, it expresses our prospects for a future together. It enunciates the way we see ourselves as a people and as a nation. The Meech Lake Accord has been scrutinized by the joint Senate-House Committee, which received 301 submissions and heard testimony, I am told, from 131 groups and individuals-from every walk of life, from every segment of our society.
The committee concluded that the Accord should be adopted by Parliament because, and I quote them:
It "represents a reasonable and workable package of constitutional reforms".
I want to pay tribute to the committee and its co-chairmen, the Hon. Member for Cambridge (Mr. Speyer), and Senator Arthur Tremblay, for their distinguished contribution to the national life of Canada.
Hear, hear.

And, Mr. Speaker, I also pay tribute to a Senator, something we do not do very often in the House these days, but I am referring to a Conservative Senator, the Minister of State for Federal-Provincial Relations, the Hon. Lowell Murray, who played an absolutely vital role on behalf of the federal Government in this great undertaking.
Hear, hear.

Mr. Speaker, I followed the committee's work quite closely and noticed a common thread running through the weeks of testimony. Canadians know that, without
October 21, 1987

the willing assent of Quebec, our Constitution is fundamentally flawed. Deep down inside, every Canadian knows that. Certain promises were made to Quebecers at the time of the 1980 referendum, solemn promises about constitutional renewal, which were not kept, unfortunately. With the Meech Lake Accord, that promise, made to Quebec on behalf of all parliamentarians, has been honoured on terms that are good for all Canadians. And I think it is a significant aspect of our debate because, Mr. Speaker, we have not acted with haste, nor have we improvised the results, as the NDP Leader indicated.
The Meech Lake Accord culminates more than two decades of intense constitutional debate in this country. Its elements are not new. As my friend the Hon. Member for Ottawa- Vanier (Mr. Gauthier), the Chief Whip of the Liberal Party, reminded his former Leader when he appeared before the committee, the Hon. Member said, and I quote:
As I remembered, you mentioned restricting the federal government's spending power; you talked about granting effective concurrent jurisdiction in the field of immigration and in Quebec, there were the Cullen-Couture agreements. You suggested provincial participation in Senate appointments. Your aim, expressed in different bills and your personal convictions, was to allow the regions to have a voice in Parliament.
But the Hon. Member for Ottawa-Vanier, a distinguished parliamentarian, might have added that the former Prime Minister had also proposed provincial involvement in Supreme Court appointments and at the 1980 round of constitutional talks he was prepared, and I quote him, "to recognize the distinct French-speaking society centred in though not confined to Quebec " in the constitution. How can it be wrong now when it was proper then? And 1 commend the Hon. Member for Ottawa-Vanier for his outstanding contribution.
Hear, hear.

The fact was, however, Mr. Speaker, these earlier proposals did not meet with success, and no one should underestimate the grave risks we ran as a country with Quebec left on the constitutional sidelines, as a result.
As the Hon. Robert Stanfield told the committee: In 1982 we created two Canadas, one that felt bound by the agreement and another that did not. Only Quebec's agenda was not addressed in the 1982 Accord. Only Quebec was left out. I ask, how would we all have felt had the concerns of women, aboriginal people and multicultural Canadians not been addressed in 1982? I ask all Members of the House to consider the sadness and sense of exclusion the people of Ontario would have felt if such basic constitutional arrangements in 1982 had been entered into without the approval of their elected representatives at Queen's Park. I tell you, Mr. Speaker, that I would never have agreed to a constitution that left Ontario on
Constitution Amendment, 1987
the sidelines, and I have worked hard to correct a similar situation regarding Quebec.
Although legally binding, the 1982 Accord did not bind the hearts and minds of Quebecers to Canada. The consequences in a generation or two may have been absolutely incalculable for all Canadians representing all regions of this House from the Gaspe to the coast of British Columbia. Imagine the possibility of another referendum on independence in Quebec where the Prime Minister of Canada would enter the campaign and solemnly promise on behalf of all Canadians to renew the Constitution. The leader of the anti-Canada forces would only have to say that Quebecers had heard such promises once before from a Canadian Prime Minister and were not about to be fooled a second time. What would the federalist forces say to that? What would be said of us for failing to seize this moment at this unique time in our history? What would be said of those in this House of Commons who did not act judiciously as the incomplete Constitution with which we were all left inexorably gave rise to separate Canadas?
In reopening the constitutional debate, in renewing the constitutional process, we had both an opportunity and, I think, on behalf of the people of Canada, an obligation. The opportunity was to seek Quebec's signature on our Constitution on terms that were fair to all regions and that built on the substantial achievements of 1982, patriation, the Charter and the amending formula. Unless we believe in a country whose Constitution represents two-thirds of the population, unless we believe in the emergence of two Canadas, our obligation was to secure Quebec's signature on terms consistent with the national interest. I sought that opportunity as Leader of my Party. I undertook that obligation as Prime Minister of Canada, and on behalf of all Members of Parliament I believe we have delivered on that commitment to all the people of Canada.
Today I wish to speak to both my colleagues in the House and to our fellow citizens in the country. All of us have come to this place with our own perspective and our own sense of Canada, with our own view of the country. This House gives us a unique perspective on our vast and diverse country, a national outlook fully consistent with our roots and origins. Wherever we come from, whatever our outlook, we all love Canada. The voices we hear every day in this House are the voices of Canadians in English and French, in idioms that also celebrate the multicultural diversity of our people.

Mr. Speaker, I cannot imagine too many countries where a fundamental question of nationhood-such as the one posed in Quebec during the referendum-would have been resolved in a fully peaceful and democratic manner. For those Canadians who also call ourselves Quebecers, it was a most remarkable experience. We all remember the solemn undertaking given on

October 21, 1987
Constitution Amendment, 1987
May 14, 1980, at the Paul Sauve Arena, by the Prime Minister of Canada-whom I approved indeed, whom we all approved-on behalf of the Government and people of Canada, and I quote him, "to renew the Constitution". But something else was said that night, and all Quebecers, all Canadians, can still remember these words, and I quote: "We, the Quebec MP's" he said "Are laying ourselves on the line, because we are telling Quebecers to vote no. And we are telling you in the other provinces that we will not agree to your interpreting a no vote as an indication that everything is fine and can remain as it was before. We want change and we are willing to lay our seats in the House on the line to have change" he said.
Mr. Speaker, six days later, in a great springtime of hope for our country, Quebecers did say no to separation. But that affirmation of confidence in Canada was never redeemed. In the constitutional discussions that followed the referendum, and I do not pass a value judgment on anybody's motives, the fact is that after the constitutional debates that followed the referendum Quebec was left isolated and alone. The eloquent promise made on the eve of the referendum to a whole population remained unfulfilled. All Quebecers longed to put these bitter divisions behind them, and it remained for those of us in public life to find a way.
At Sept-Iles on August 6, 1984, I made a pledge of my own, to seek Quebec's signature on the Constitution, on terms that it could sigh "with honour and enthusiasm". I believe the manner in which the members of the Quebec National Assembly said yes to Canada is evident testimony to the genuineness of their commitment and their willingness to enshrine it. All of us will always remember the words of Premier Bourassa at the signing ceremony on June 3, when he said, and I quote: "It is with great pride as a Quebecer and as a Canadian that I am here today to express my deep satisfaction with the re-integration of Quebec within the Canadian Constitution".

I can tell you, Mr. Speaker, it was a long time since I or anyone else had heard a Premier of Quebec make such a profound commitment to Canada, and when that takes place all Canadians, and the profound sentiments of Canadian unity, benefit from one coast of Canada to the other.
I also support the Meech Lake Accord because it corresponds as best it can, as the Leader of the New Democratic Party pointed out, with how we can organize the affairs of our federation and how we can try to live together as Canadians. The Hon. Eric Kierans, who served with distinction at both levels of government in the Lesage and Trudeau Cabinets, captured, I think, the essence of the Accord when he said:
I am for Meech Lake because it is the closest that we have ever come to the division of powers enshrined in the British North America Act and the real spirit of that Act.
At Sept-lles I undertook to establish a federal-provincial advisory and co-ordinating body which would operate at the
highest levels and seek to harmonize the policies of the two levels of government and respect provincial jurisdiction. I believe the Meech Lake constitutional Accord translates that vision of Canada into reality.
Federal-provincial relations need not be a theatre for dramatic and sterile posturing. They can become, as we are witnessing, with the co-operation of all of the First Ministers, a unique laboratory for effective and productive economic and social action.
1 have spoken of the historic opportunity presented by this Accord, but we are no less aware of solemn obligations, in the eyes of our fellow citizens and in the eyes of history itself. It is the obligation of Parliament and the Government, and the solemn duty of the Prime Minister, to uphold the national interest. It is equally the duty of Parliament, the Government, and the Prime Minister to protect the rights of individuals and groups who compose our society. For as one of our founding fathers, George Etienne Cartier, observed over a century ago:
In a country such as ours, all rights must be safeguarded, just as all convictions must be respected.
I think the Meech Lake Accord is very much in harmony with those principles. It builds upon and in no way negates the significant achievements of 1982, including the Charter of Rights and Freedoms. As the joint committee notes, the recognition of duality and Quebec's distinct society will not "have the effect of justifying an erosion of bilingualism or charter rights, or lead to a denial of multiculturalism".
In the view of the First Ministers, all of them, according to the Government's best legal advice, and consistent with the preponderance of expert legal testimony at the hearings, nothing in this Accord overrides the guarantees of the Charter, or takes away in any way from minority language rights, equality rights for women, or Canada's multicultural heritage.
Hear, hear!

That is the best expert opinion. That is our intent in presenting the Accord. That is our commitment.
Let there be no misunderstanding whatsoever. In voting for this Accord, Members are upholding the rights of our language minorities, English-speaking in Quebec and Frenchspeaking outside Quebec. Let no one misconstrue our commitment, either now or at any time in the future. If I, for one moment, thought that anyone's rights were being overridden by this Accord, I would not have recommended it to my colleagues in Government, and the Government of Canada would never have brought it forward for consideration in Parliament today.
In my maiden address in this House, on the Manitoba language question, I said that in my judgment there is no obligation more compelling and no duty more irresistible in Canada than to ensure that our minorities, linguistic and otherwise, live at all times in conditions of fairness and justice.
October 21, 1987

That remains my view today, and I know it is the view of every single Member of this Elouse.
Hear, hear!

As many people have noted and as many observers have commented upon, we are already reaping the benefits of a stronger and more united Canada.

On September 1, in Quebec, I met with Premier Bourassa prior to the Francophone Summit, in itself another event which relates to national reconciliation, a very significant event in terms of the French dimension of our international personality. I was especially struck by something he said on that occasion: "Never have we known a period of national solidarity as profound as that which we are experiencing today," he observed. I applaud the Premier, and all his colleagues, for their statesmanship and vision. Individually and as a group, the First Ministers had the courage, and summoned the political will, to do the right thing for Canada.

On behalf of all parliamentarians I salute all First Ministers who participated in this noble objective.

Hear, hear!

Indeed, Mr. Speaker, they are mature men, sensitive and intelligent human beings, and all Premiers knew that as long as Quebec was absent from the table, the Constitution Act of 1982 was dangerously incomplete. And they knew that as long as Quebec was absent, the constitutional process could not go forward on other important issues such as Senate reform, aboriginal rights and fisheries.

With the Accord, Quebec comes back to the constitutional table and back to the table of the Canadian family. In supporting the Accord we are opening the door to future constitutional reform. For example, without the participation of Quebec, reform of the Senate was both legally and politically impossible. You can talk about it all you want, but it could not have taken place in the absence of Quebec.
On the question of aboriginal rights we came very, very close to achieving a resolution of the principal issue at the 1985 First Ministers' Conference. It is my view that we would have come much closer, given the track record of succeeding Quebec Governments on this very sensitive issue, indeed we probably would have succeeded in 1985, had Quebec been part of the process at that time. Justice would have been achieved for our aboriginal peoples, at least in a substantial measure, two years ago. We must now, in my judgment, manage this issue with great care, as we have done with the Quebec Round.
We are continuing to discuss with aboriginal groups a number of important ideas for a fresh start on constitutional recognition of self-government, as well as the question of
Constitution Amendment, 1987
constitutional funding. Most of all, as we tried to do in the Quebec Round, we have to get together as parliamentarians to create a climate that can help to ensure success in bringing justice to our native peoples.

Mr. Speaker, on the important question of gender equality rights, the Joint Committee notes: "We do not believe that the entrenchment of the distinct society duality clause will in any realistic way erode the present constitutional protections of individuals rights, including gender equality rights." I refer Hon. Members to the testimony before the Joint Committee of Mrs. Francine McKenzie, President of the Quebec Advisory Council on the Status of Women, who shares this view, and to the remarkable comments made by my friend, the NDP Member from British Columbia, who has shown strong leadership in this case as in many others. This is what Mrs. McKenzie said:
Let me remind you that it was because of the special request made by women's groups in 1982 that section 28 was put into the Canadian Charter. In this way, the right to equality came foremost in the constitutional hierarchy and thus for the past five years it has been clear that the constitutional rights and freedoms granted to the men and women of Canada must at all times be exercised in equality.
In my opinion, Mr. Speaker, it is a telling argument. [English]
On the question of the Territories, the joint committee noted that their residents will continue to be constitutionally eligible for appointment to the Senate and the Supreme Court. The Government shares this view and agrees with the committee that First Ministers may wish to examine the matter at future constitutional conferences. This Government will continue to encourage the political evolution of Canada's North. Indeed, we are taking steps to facilitate and accelerate that evolution which will contribute to a much stronger nation.
In perhaps a more general way I would refer Hon. Members to the comments of the Hon. Jack Pickersgill, former Clerk of the Privy Council, Principal Secretary to the Prime Minister, and a senior cabinet Minister who served four Liberal Prime Ministers and Canada with enormous distinction and accomplishment. I am sure there are Conservatives, no longer in this House, who would not agree entirely with that statement because, among other things, Mr. Pickersgill was a most accomplished parliamentarian who took it out on many Tories and a few New Democrats as well. Given his life's work and his tremendous contribution to Canada, I was particularly interested in some comments he made shortly after Meech Lake. He wrote: "On the eve of that meeting," in reference to Meech Lake, "I would not have given the First Ministers one chance in ten of success. I was excited and delighted when they reached accord. Once I read the document I was satisfied it met the requirements of Quebec without in any way reducing the jurisdiction of the Parliament of Canada. I was delighted

October 21, 1987
Constitution Amendment, 1987
by the generous and united reception of the miracle of Meech Lake by all Parties in Parliament".
Mr. Pickersgill later said: "If we allow this opportunity to pass, my guess is that it will probably not arise again for another generation, and never again will it arise on such reasonable terms". I agree with Mr. Pickersgill on that. It was for us to seize the moment. It is a great tribute to all Members of the House of Commons that we have done just that.
Hear, hear!

This is about Canada. Although, obviously, the object of the exercise was to bring Quebec back into the fold, we have achieved many gains for Canada with the Meech Lake Accord. We have obtained the return of Quebec to the Canadian constitutional family-a pretty important event- with honour and enthusiasm. One would not want another backing into an important situation of this kind. There had to be the pride, the dignity and the acknowledgement of Quebec's unique role in our development, and that requires enthusiasm. It requires the output of one's mind, but also the output of one's heart.
We have reaffirmed the principle of the equality of provinces, large and small. Since when does Alberta have to be a second-class province in this regard, or British Columbia, compared to some other provinces? Under this agreement all the provinces are equal irrespective of size. I think that is a tremendous affirmation of what we truly believe in in the House of Commons.
As my friend, the Leader of the New Democratic Party, has pointed out, we have, very importantly, for the first time, given constitutional recognition to the federal spending power. We entrenched our commitment for the next round on Senate reform and other issues in our ongoing constitutional process. Canada's First Ministers said all along right from the beginning that if no egregious error was found in the text, we would proceed with the resolution. There are complaints. There are concerns. There are suggestions. But no such egregious error has been indicated.
I can tell you, Mr. Speaker, without hesitation, that the Government of Canada is not prepared to jeopardize this act of national reconciliation by reopening for renegotiation virtually every section of the Accord, as some would have us do. We believe that this is very much in the national interest of Canada, and we are bringing it forward in that light.

Mr. Speaker, the Meech Lake Accord is not only a sound document-it is one that conforms to a consistent, generous and logical vision of Canada. It respects the equality of Provinces and values the distinctiveness Quebec brings to Canada. It specifically reaffirms the strength and the leadership of the national Government in the great constitutional debate. Quite obviously, the Accord is not perfect. But if we
wait for perfection, we risk undoing what has been accomplished and will make no progress at all.

I urge the House to adopt this resolution. The Quebec National Assembly and the Saskatchewan Legislature have already ratified the Meech Lake Accord. I suggest that the House and other legislatures adopt the resolution in exactly the same spirit.
I support the Meech Lake Accord because it is a time for healing in this country. It is a time for redeeming solemn pledges. It is a time for Members of Parliament and Canadians to take the long view of history. It is a time for federal arrangements which better reflect the very nature of our country and the sentiments of our people. It is a time for making Canada whole again. It is a time for putting the divisions of the past behind us so that we can, as a united country, meet the challenges of an increasingly complex and interdependent world.
It is a time to continue the task of building one Canada, united and strong. That is what Meech Lake is all about-one Canada. We saw the emergence of two, and this is about one, built on tolerance, fairness and generosity for all Canadians.
Hear, hear!

I stand where every Prime Minister from Sir John right through to Mr. Diefenbaker have stood on behalf of my Party and all Parties in this House. All Prime Ministers have been motivated by the concept of the integrity of this country, one Canada. The possible emergence of two was something that had to be dealt with firmly, fairly, equitably and with generosity and vision. That is what leadership is about. This House is invited to take a great act of national leadership and bring Canadians from one end of the country to the other together again in one-
[ Translation]
-one Canada, united, strong and prosperous. And that is what Meech Lake is really about!
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, it is an honour and a privilege for me to follow the Leader of the New Democratic Party (Mr. Broadbent) and the Prime Minister in this most important debate. By speaking today, they have both done a lot for Canadian unity.
I would like to begin my comments by quoting the words of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Hnatyshyn), who said the following in his speech of September 29:
Canada is a partnership of its peoples and provinces, a partnership which can be willingly embraced but not imposed. This concept is understood and accepted by Canadians from coast to coast.
As I rise in this House today to support the adoption of the Meech Lake Accord, I have to ask myself, after listening to some of my colleagues, whether they have really understood
October 21, 1987

and accepted the quite accurate definition given by the Minister of Justice of the nature of Canada. Our country is a federation, a political system comprised of two levels of Government which must complete and complement each other to serve the population. It is a delicate union of often very different people spread out regionally over an immense continent. Indeed, it is a union which has defied all logic for over 120 years.
We have to marvel at the fact that, throughout our history, we have always been able to solve our problems and settle our differences relatively peacefully. As we know, other countries have had wars and revolutions, but not Canada.
While I fought vigorously against them politically, I must say that I have always admired the democratic understanding of the supporters of independence in Quebec. Mr. Rene Levesque and his supporters used elections and a referendum to try to achieve victory for their political ideals. They did not succeed. However, to defeat them, their opponents had promised in May of 1980 a renewed federalism and a new, updated Constitution which would take into account the legitimate aspirations of the various partners in our federation.
That was the beginning of the great constitutional debate of the early 1980s, which led finally, after many years of frustration, to patriation of our Constitution and to entrenchment of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, which was a major achievement.
I do not have enough time here to pay tribute as much as I would have liked to the former Prime Minister, Pierre Elliott Trudeau. However, I shall simply say that, because of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, he will be remembered as one of the greatest Prime Ministers of Canada, if not the greatest. On the other hand, while the Constitution Act of 1982 was the crowning achievement for some people, it was unfortunately for many others a show of strength and an agreement excluding Quebec.
In the euphoria of success, we federal Liberals did not fully realize the bitterness of those who had been left out.
We rationalized this situation at that time by saying that the PQ would never have agreed anyway. But they were not alone in condemning this agreement passed without the consent of Quebec's duly elected Government. This explains why the Members of Quebec's National Assembly, PQs and Liberals alike, voted against the agreement. 1 will even say that, intoxicated with this success, we invited Her Majesty the Queen to come over and celebrate with us this triumph, although she was in the eyes of several opponents at that time the living symbol of colonialism.
Because the constitutional issue had become an open sore, it had to be treated. It had to heal as soon as possible. The Leader of the Conservative Party, for one, was well aware of
Constitution Amendment, 1987
the need to have it healed. He should be commended for having stated in Sept-Iles in August of 1984, and I quote:
We must make commitments and take concrete steps to achieve the goal which I have set for myself and which I repeat today: convince Quebec's National Assembly to approve with pride and enthusiasm the new Canadian Constitution.
This is also what Premier Bourassa had in mind when he stated the five conditions which he insisted had to be met before the Government of Quebec could adhere to the Constitutional Act and when he sent Mr. Remillard, his Minister responsible for Canadian Intergovernmental Affairs on a tour of the provincial capitals to explain Quebec's proposals.
As a matter of fact, Senator Tremblay emphasized this on August 27. I think I should quote part from his remarks to show how we came about getting the accord we are dealing with today. He said:
What has specifically happened is that Mr. Bourassa's current Quebec government, having set out a number of points in its election campaign-five, which resurfaced later-and having thus obtained an unquestioned mandate from the Quebec people, embarked on the process which has brought us to the Meech Lake Accord; in exchange all the other partners were obliged to make a major concession: specifically, to respect these five points. It happened that the reasonableness of Quebec's proposals made it possible for an accord to be reached.
This is what was also understood by my leader, the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner), when in May of 1986 he publically accepted in an article published in Le Devoir Mr. Bourassa's five proposals, and made a commitment to have that new constitutional position recognized within the Liberal Party of Canada. Thus the Meech Lake Accord is the response to Mr. Bourassa's proposals. It complements the 1982 Constitutional Act. Our work remained incomplete because Quebec had not signed. Because of that serious shortcoming, this country did not really constitute a whole as we would have liked. The work had to be completed.
The Leader of the Opposition had promised to do so as soon as he would be re-elected Prime Minister. However, this Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) did it before him, because it must be recognized that all English-speaking Premiers wanted to see that page turned.
Mr. Levesque claimed he was betrayed by the latter in 1982, and I am convinced the English-speaking Premiers were eager to make good to Quebec. Such a feeling certainly made things easier for the Prime Minister. Surely we must give the Prime Minister credit for the work he did, but for modesty's sake he must recognize that the success has to be shared with the Leader of the Opposition who took the political sting out of that debate and who very early made it clear that if he were Prime Minister, just like the present Prime Minister, that matter had to be solved. And certainly the Prime Minister will accept to share the limelight with Quebec's Premier, because as Senator Tremblay reminded us, without the specific, clear and bounded proposals of the Quebec Government, it would

October 21, 1987
Constitution Amendment, 1987
have been excessively difficult to reach this constitutional accord.
1 know the Leader of the Opposition spoke to his colleagues, the Liberal Premiers who were parties to the agreement. I know he even spoke with the Premier of his own Province of British Columbia to make sure there would be that spirit of cooperation and understanding to reach a compromise, a honourable compromise for Quebec.
In any event, this should come as no surprise, because national interest always transcends political groups. Was Prime Minister Trudeau not assured of the support of Premiers Bill Davis and Richard Hatfield when he started off on his historical process of patriating the Canadian Constitution?
This is why I do not hesitate to say today that the Prime Minister did what was to be done to bring Quebec back as a full partner into Canada. Some people suggest the Prime Minister made too many concessions to get that agreement. My answer is no. First, as suggested by the Leader of the Opposition in his speech of September 29, 1987, the Canadian Government keeps its leadership role within Confederation and loses none of the powers it already has under the Canadian Constitution.
Second, when we take an impartial look at the main provisions of the Meech Lake Agreement, it must be recognized that this kind of give and take, under one form or another, already had been proposed by the previous Liberal Government. In fact, those provisions relating to immigration only enshrine some administrative arrangements agreed to by the former Liberal Government and implemented successively in the following agreements: Lang-Cloutier in 1971, Andras-Bienvenue in 1975 and Cullen-Couture in 1979. We, in the Liberal party, would be ill-advised to pretend it is a bad thing.
As a Quebecker and member from Quebec, I am happy with the provisions relating to the Supreme Court because they definitely guarantee the appointment of at least three judges from the Quebec civil law system. This practice has existed for a long time but from now on, it will be a constitutional rule. As well, provinces will now be involved in the selection of members of our highest court. I suggest this is quite appropriate in a federal state and I do not think it is an unreasonable concession.
Then, the Accord states that, until the Constitution is amended in order to reform the Senate fundamentally, provincial Governments will also be directly involved in the appointment of Senators. This is perhaps the part of the Accord that I like least, because no deadline has been set for that desirable reform of the Senate. Therefore, with time, provincial Premiers might come to like these appointments and forget that long-overdue reform. I might add that although I am not pleased, we should not forget nevertheless that the Senate was originally established to reflect precisely provincial interests in the Parliament of Canada and that the former Liberal Government was even willing to let at some time the
provinces appoint half of Canadian Senators. It is therefore difficult to believe that this initiative goes too far. It can hardly be claimed, I think.
In addition, the Accord deals with new procedures between Ottawa and the provinces for the establishment of future costsharing programs and it allows provinces to opt out with compensation in specific circumstances. Some people fear that provision of the Accord might put an end to major Canadian social programs. I, for one, do not agree with that view. The people's will and the real and pressing needs of Canadian citizens will always win over politicians concerned by their reelection. By the way, the Minister of Justice has well summarized that part of the agreement when he said, and I quote: "This is clearly an area where federal and provincial powers overlap and therefore it is necessary to negotiate accommodations to ensure co-operation and avoid court contests. Such plans can only work with the genuine support of both the federal and provincial Governments, and jurisdictional issues must be avoided in the interest of those who are to benefit from such plans."
In my opinion, this is not an excessive concession but merely an expression of wisdom.
The Accord also provides that a greater number of subjects will require unanimity for amendments and it specifies that there will be annual conferences of First Ministers on constitutional matters.
When I came to Ottawa in 1964 to work for the Minister of Justice, Hon. Guy Favreau, he was working hard to have the provinces agree to a patriation and amending formula. It was the Fulton-Favreau formula, as it was called in those days. Many more procedures have been suggested since then, including the Victoria and the Meech Lake formulas. As a matter of fact, all the successive federal and provincial Ministers of Justice have tried to find one. I sometimes get the impression that a constitutional lawyer must be hiding behind every politician. That is why I am convinced that the search for the ideal formula will go on for years and that many interesting suggestions will come up.
What is before us today is the Meech Lake formula. It reflects the very simple reality that all provinces are equal, regardless of their size, numbers and year of entry in the Canadian federation. Personally, I cannot help but think that the rule of unanimity must prevail, in all justice, for the amendment of some basic institutions in this country. This is not compromise but simply fairness. It may be an exaggeration to have annual First Ministers Conferences to discuss constitutional matters. Once a year may be too much. And discussing fisheries year in and year out may seem a bit ridiculous. But politics is the art of compromise. And if this is the price that the Prime Minister had to pay to convince Newfoundland to support the inclusion of Quebec into the Canadian Constitution, I might find that rather ludicrous, but I cannot hold it
October 21, 1987

against him because he did not abdicate the federal jurisdiction in the area of fisheries, contrary to what some are alleging.
Last, there is in the Accord an interpretation clause which formerly recognizes two basic realities: the linguistic duality of Canada and the distinct identity of the Province of Quebec. Let us consider for a while the crux of the issue, the bone of contention, that is to say the recognition of Quebec's distinct character. In fact, this is the issue which has raised the most heated discussions during this debate. The roots of Quebec's specificity, to paraphrase a term used in the Pepin-Robarts report, are older than Canada itself. The witnesses who have appeared before the Joint Committee on Constitution of the Senate and the House of Commons pointed out that the legal basis of that notion dated back to the year 1713 at least. Thus, the co-existence of two distinct communities was formerly recognized. Others have pointed out that the Treaty of Paris, in 1763, and the edicts of various British governors recognized certain religious and linguistic rights as well as legal rights for the allocation of new lands, according to what they called "the French laws".
As a consequence, throughout our history, the distinctive and actual presence of a francophone community living in a given geographic area affected the legal and institutional structures governing it.
Those institutional frameworks, including the British-North America Act, have progressively allowed the blossoming of a modern French society in America.
As Mr. Claude Ryan said in his Beige Book, and I quote:
In the Province of Quebec, the laws, legal system, municipal and provincial institutions, voluntary organizations, media, arts, literature, educational system, social and health services, religious institutions and credit unions are mostly French by reason of the language and the culture that permeate them. So, Quebec is, within the Canadian federation, a distinct society due to its language, culture, institutions and life-style.
This recognition of Quebec as a distinct society was Premier Bourassa's first and most important prerequisite. All four claims were accepted, but for all provinces. First, there was the issue of extended powers for Quebec in immigration matters, and this was also offered to the other provinces; second, limitation of the spending power of the federal Government, which obviously does not apply only to Quebec, but to all other provinces wishing to opt out of various programs; third, the new procedure to amend the Constitution, which provides a veto for Quebec and which also applies to the other provinces; and finally, the participation of Quebec in the appointment of judges, which also applies to the other provinces.
However, the distinct identity clause is special and applies only to Quebec. I must say that this major claim could not be rejected. The Prime Minister and the Premiers recognized that fact, and at this time, I feel that I must pay hommage to three of my colleagues who could have objected to the Accord, but who, with generosity and an open mind, have decided to support it. I am thinking especially about the Hon. Member
Constitution Amendment, 1987
for Notre-Dame-de-Grace (Mr. Allmand) who represents, in my opinion, the increasingly tolerant and understanding views of the English-speaking minority in Quebec. In this regard, the Hon. Member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace is in agreement with Alliance Quebec, the major movement which defends the English-speaking minority in Quebec and which was not afraid to assert that it was in favour of recognizing the distinct identity of Quebec.
I also wish to pay hommage to two Members who represent the French-speaking minorities outside Quebec, my colleague for Ottawa-Vanier and my colleague for Glengarry- Prescott-Russell, both of whom could have said: Something is being done for Quebec, but not for us, French-speaking minorities outside Quebec, and we want it to happen immediately. However, just like the organization which represents all French-speaking Canadians outside Quebec, the Association des francophones hors Quebec, which appeared before the Joint Committee of the Senate and the Flouse of Commons, they were magnanimous enough to say that recognizing the distinct identity of Quebec would not reduce by any means the development opportunities of French-speaking minorities outside Quebec.
I therefore salute these three Members of my caucus who could have taken different stands, but who had the openmindedness to accept that, at this historic moment, we should say yes to Quebec at a time when conditions are the most favorable even to achieve an accord which will give a generous place to Quebec in Canada, and when, under the leadership of Premier Robert Bourassa, at whose abilities I grow more and more pleasantly surprised every day, Quebec is going through a period of peace and moderation and its demands have never been as reasonable.
In the final analysis, that Accord is good for Canada because it is good for Quebec. It may not be perfect and there will always be room for improvement, but it is the best deal that could be negotiated at this time by the Prime Minister of Canada and all Premiers.
Some of my colleagues who are opposed to this Accord or who have some concerns about it should remember that even former Prime Minister Trudeau and his Minister of Justice, Mr. Jean Chretien, have not made a perfect deal in 1982. They did not solve the problem of native people. They even had to grant major concessions, such as the notwithstanding clause or the "where numbers warrant" rule. However, they agreed to that deal because it was the best possible one at the time. Then, they were certainly very happy with their achievement that despite concessions and some compromise granted, because in their mind, it was a huge step forward in the constitutional area and they were right to think so. Today, some concessions have had to be made. Some adjustments have had to be left aside. Certainly the Prime Minister and the Premiers have not solved everything during the Meech Lake meeting, but they still have made a deal that will be another major step forward in the constitutional area.

October 21, 1987
Constitution Amendment, 1987
Recently I read the special issue of Life magazine on the American Constitution. In February, 1787, the American Congress instructed the delegates of the 13 states to devise measures to render the federal Constitution adequate to the exigencies of the Union. They assembled in Philadelphia, and for four months they worked diligently in camera to produce a 4,400 word document that is a remarkable achievement, even after two centuries.
Interestingly enough, there was a very strong opposition to the ratification of this text. Those who prepared it were saying: "It is a genuine compromise, you have to take it as a package. Now is not the time to amend it, it is the time to ratify it, otherwise the union will fall apart, and we may never have another occasion to get such a deal".
Those who were opposing it felt that it was not perfect, it should be amended. Too many things were left out, and they were predicting that, if ratified, things would not work out and it would be the end of the Union.
When I was reading the article, I thought I was reading the history of the Canadian Meech Lake Accord. Well, as you know it was ratified. The Union did not fall apart. Soon thereafter a Bill of Rights was added to the Constitution. Over the years, as the United States of America grew and prospered, 16 more amendments were added.
Among those who favoured the Accord were Benjamin Franklin, James Madison, and George Washington, all of whom have a prominent place in the history of the United States.
Who remembers today those who opposed the Accord? Very few. They were so wrong; they had such a defaitiste attitude that nobody wants to remember Elbridge Gerry or Patrick Henry.
[ Translation]
To conclude, I want to say that I know that my Leader, the Opposition Leader, would like to amend the Meech Lake Accord to make it more acceptable for more Canadians. That is fine if it can be done. Otherwise, as he said himself, and I quote: "If our amendments are rejected and voted down, we intend to make these amendments part of our Party's constitutional program. We intend to make them part of the platform in the next federal election and put them before the people of Canada. If and when we form a government, we intend to make them part of the ongoing constitutional process."
The Opposition Leader is right to say that, much remains to be done. I am very glad he thus clearly established the future constitutional agenda, and I hope that under his leadership, the aboriginal people will finally obtain what they want, the Senate will become an elected body, Canada's North may have a chance to prosper under the aegis of the provinces and that
Canada's multicultural minorities will be even better protected. This is a long-range project reflecting a very clear understanding of where subsequent constitutional reforms should lead us. I may add that although the Leader of the Opposition would like to make some major changes in this document, he had the courage and strength of character to say that if those amendments were not adopted now, he would nevertheless vote in favour of the Meech Lake Accord, and I think he is to be commended for saying so. I want to say that, as a Quebecer and a Canadian, I am very proud of the Leader of the Opposition.
Parliamentarians should forget past struggles and partisan considerations and take advantage of the unique opportunity we now have in this country to say yes to Quebec. That is why I will vote for the Accord, although I realize there is room for improvement and that there are some oversights and shortcomings. I will vote for the Accord, because the Meech Lake Accord is based on a philosophy that is broad and generous enough to accept the distinct character of a province that was fully aware of its identity but failed to obtain formal recognition of that fact. I would go so far as to say, and in fact I am convinced, that this will increase the confidence of Quebecers in the legitimacy of the federal system. To me it is obvious that our country will be more united if the role and specific place of Quebec in Canada are fully recognized.
Mr. Speaker, 1 fully appreciate the concerns expressed with vigour and conviction by some of my colleagues, especially in my own Party. I believe those concerns reflect the intrinsic complexity of constitutional reform. I acknowledge and respect their convictions, because as Machiavelli once said: "Nothing in the world is more difficult to grasp, more perilous to undertake or less likely to succeed than the desire to reform the constitutional system of a State."
Though these words were said in Florence about 500 years ago, they are still true today, in our country as in many others.
Mr. Speaker, Renan described a nation as a daily plebiscite. He stressed that to be a nation, a people must clearly express its desire to live together. During the Referendum, Quebecers expressed that desire, and seven years later, the Meech Lake Accord is a new reflection of that desire. Seven years later, Mr. Speaker, I want to say to every Member in this House and especially the Members of my own Party that all of Canada must say yes. And that is why I fully support the Meech Lake Accord.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, I join in the debate today realizing that it is the end of a full day of debate which has included some very special presentations on the Meech Lake Accord by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), by the Leader of the New Democratic Party (Mr. Broadbent),
October 21, 1987

and by the Hon. Member for Papineau (Mr. Ouellet) of the Official Opposition.
I come to this debate with a kind of special background. I am one of those elected by the community of Montreal whose first language is English. As the Hon. Member for Lachine 1 am particularly pleased to have the occasion to share in this historic debate. Lachine provides an excellent example of Canada's two cultures living and working in co-operation. It reflects a wide range of opinions and a mixture of economic and multicultural heritages.
1 also come to the debate today as a member of the special joint committee which was established to review the Meech Lake Accord and the representations regarding constitutional change. I spent many hours with that committee over weeks of hearings, hearing and reading informed opinions and concerns of Canadians. I can report that the witnesses who appeared before us were virtually unanimous in their agreement with the important and desirable goal of having Quebec willingly and honourably rejoining the Canadian constitutional family.
Finally, as an active member of the English-speaking community of Quebec and as a proud third generation Canadian, 1 feel that it deserves my best effort to be a responsible representative of the community which I serve.
In 1984, Canadians elected a Conservative Government to fulfil its publicly announced mandate. The unification of Canada was one of our first priorities, together with enhanced trade, tax reform, a defence policy, improved social programs, and the introduction of fiscal responsibility to government. The first objective, the objective of uniting Canada, required a constitutional process to bring Quebec into the family willingly and honourably. I believe that all Quebec Members of Parliament support this fundamental objective to be part of a country with full commitment to the Constitution.
I should like to refer to the words of Peter Meekison when he said:
I feel very strongly that Quebec must be part of the Constitution. Moreover, it is not just being part of it. It is sitting around a table like this and having full participation by the Quebec Government.
I have been involved in this process since 1969 and 1 know what a significant contribution to the over-all debate Quebecers can make and to have them sit there and not participate, to me, is a tragedy.
After appraising all the opinions and comments of the witnesses, I am satisfied that the process of getting Canada and Quebec reunited has not come at the expense of the rights and interests of the English population which I represent. In fact, let there be no misunderstanding. By supporting the Meech Lake Accord I am saying yes to Quebec, yes to Canada and yes to the protection of minority language rights for all Canadians. All Quebecers, both English and French-speaking, share the essential need to have Quebec as full partner in Canada.
Constitution Amendment, 1987
I was attracted to a new issue of the magazine put out by the Commissioner for Official Languages. It arrived at my desk this week. Its title is Language and Society. There are a number of articles on our Meech Lake Accord. In the summaries of this new series and new magazine that all can read, and I hope people will, such thoughts are recorded as:
Public opinion, particularly among the younger generations, is increasingly supportive of the country's linguistic duality. Despite this, linguistic prejudice still raises its head from time to time in some parts of Canada.
Another comment reads:
Our minority language groups are still in a precarious situation. Far too many Canadians still do not enjoy the linguistic guarantees provided in the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, especially in the educational area.
It goes on:
Canada is far from being the only country in the world searching for wise and reasonable solutions to the kinds of conflicts that can set language communities at odds.
One of the comments in a letter to the editor to welcoming the new format of the magazine comes from Royal Orr, President, Alliance Quebec. He says that the new Language and Society magazine:
-is good news for all Canadians interested in the promotion of both official languages.
That is just a summary, Mr. Speaker, of the views that are shared by my colleagues and neighbours in Quebec. Some are of the opinion that the Meech Lake Accord will be accompanied by a diminishing of rights of anglophone Quebecers. But these concerns have been studied by many of Canada's leading legal and constitutional experts and declared to be unfounded. It has been clearly stated by the majority of witnesses and, for that matter, by the Hon. Prime Minister and the Leaders of the opposition Parties that in their interpretation no loss of rights would be permitted by the amendments. In fact, Quebec's signature on the document of amendments to the Constitution guarantees the recognition and preservation of the English-speaking minority in Quebec as part of a fundamental characteristic of Canada. Furthermore, the amendment document goes on to say:
The role of the Parliament of Canada and the provincial legislatures shall be to preserve that fundamental characteristic mentioned above.
Constitutional change must reflect the reality and the development of Canada as a changing nation in a changing world. At the same time it must provide for growth and preservation of rights and values. The accomplishments at Meech Lake were achieved in spite of the major differences that have been expressed in advance by leaders across the country, in spite of the strong regional interests which have always been characteristic of Canada, and in spite of the many past frustrations of those who had tried to solve the problem.
In his remarks to the House earlier today, the Prime Minister quoted one of our senior parliamentarians, the Hon. Jack Pickersgill, who said that the achievements at Meech Lake were in a sense a miracle with so many differences to

October 21, 1987
Immigration Act, 1976
resolve. The results were achieved in an atmosphere which was basically are of a common commitment. We came out of the Edmonton, Alberta meeting of First Ministers a year earlier bringing Quebec into Canada and the Constitution as a first priority for Canadians and the Governments of Canada. With the leadership of our Prime Minister this was achieved at Meech Lake. It was based on an approach which is consultation and collaboration. Compromise, yes, but also trust.
I was disappointed in the hearings of the Meech Lake committee in one respect. There was not enough time for all of us to pose all the questions to the witnesses that we might have liked. In particular, I found myself prompted to want to question our past Prime Minister, Mr. Trudeau, when he was with us. He had an idea of Canada with which Canadians were not comfortable. We had come to Government with the obligation and the opportunity to change the country. I wanted to ask the previous Prime Minister, knowing his particular skills in debate and in intellectual activity, at what point of importance did he place goodwill and trust in a partnership and association that is Canada? I think that is something that has been brought by our Prime Minister to this negotiating table and to the Accord that we are now debating.
There are many essential items in the Accord. One, immigration jointly managed where the provinces wish, which is exactly in line with the agreement that had been reached between Quebec and Canada many years ago in the 1970s. Two, spending powers on federal programs within provincial jurisdiction and an automatic recognition of the rights of the provinces, leaving the need for initiative and leadership by the federal Government. Three, the appointments process to the Supreme Court of Canada and, until it is reformed, to the Senate. 1 think this was a very generous but at the same time a realistic recognition of the rights of the provinces in these two areas.
Unquestionably the section of the constitutional amendment which has prompted the greatest reaction and comment among my community has been the interpretive clauses calling for the recognition of a language duality and within Canada the distinct society of Quebec. Since the 1970s there has been no question that Quebec's English-speaking community has felt anxious with respect to its historic position.
We have had attacks on anglophone rights in the original Bill 101, Bill 22 and even to an extent today in Bill 101 with the sign concerns under both nationalist and moderate Quebec provincial Governments. Many of these fears were put to rest when, by a majority of Quebecers, we voted no to a separate Quebec and no to a divided Canada. We are proud Quebecers and aware that both communities must continue to look for the balance of mutual acceptance. Much of our community supported Mr. Bourassa in 1985 because of his commitment to find an acceptable solution with respect to bilingual signs. We look forward to his living up to those commitments.
In 1982, when we patriated the Constitution with an amending formula and our Charter of Rights, the Quebec
Government refused to participate. Since that time Canada has been, if not legally but morally, ethically and spiritually, incomplete. The Meech Lake Accord repairs the omission of 1982 and represents an historic act of reconciliation. For the first time, it explicitly recognizes the presence of English speaking persons in Quebec as an integral element of Canada's linguistic duality. Quebec's distinct society within Canada which, in my opinion, represents a fact that has been in existence for many years, includes English-speaking Quebecers. As I and much of my community have always felt, we are an essential part of Quebec's distinctiveness. The courts will now be constitutionally directed to acknowledge that reality.
The linguistic duality clause affirms Quebec's role in preserving Canada's linguistic duality. Both linguistic duality and distinct society clauses must be read and interpreted together by the courts. Quebec's role in preserving and promoting its distinct society is thus qualified by its additional role in preserving Canada's linguistic duality.
I must assure this House and the constituents of English speaking Quebec, and most importantly Lachine, that I would not be promoting the Meech Lake amendments if I felt that any rights of the community have been take away. I am confident, based on the expert legal witnesses who came before the committee, that no rights would be altered because of the amendments we have proposed.
As declared so forcefully, so passionately and so effectively by our Prime Minister, the Meech Lake Accord and the constitutional amendment gives us, all Canadians, a united country ready to live and work together for mutual advantage. It is ours. Let us make it work.
